title: What Can We Control?
content:
Throughout history, philosophers have reflected on an important question: How should we live when we cannot control everything around us?

One of the most famous philosophers, Socrates, believed that people should examine their own lives. According to Plato's account of his trial, Socrates said that an unexamined life was not worth living. In other words, he believed that people needed to question their choices, values, and actions instead of simply living without reflection.

Centuries later, the Stoic philosopher Epictetus developed a similar idea about human life and personal responsibility. He explained that some things were under our control, while others were not. He believed that our opinions, choices, and actions belonged to us, but many external events did not.

Epictetus argued that people often became unhappy because they tried to control things that were impossible to control. He suggested that individuals should focus their energy on their own decisions and attitudes instead.

These ideas can still be applied to modern life.

Imagine that someone is preparing for an important job interview. That person can study, practice answers, and arrive on time. However, they cannot completely control the interviewer's opinion or the final decision.

Socrates might have encouraged that person to reflect honestly on their preparation and motivations. Epictetus would probably have said that the person should focus on what was within their control instead of worrying excessively about the final result.

This perspective does not mean that people should stop caring about the future. Instead, it suggests that they should understand the difference between making an effort and controlling every outcome.

Perhaps this is one of philosophy's most useful lessons: we cannot always choose what happens to us, but we can reflect on how we respond.

Socrates believed that a meaningful life required examination, while Epictetus taught that inner freedom depended on understanding what truly belonged to us. Their ideas were different in many ways, but both philosophers encouraged people to look inward.

In a world full of uncertainty, their message remains relevant: we may not control everything that happens, but we can still examine our choices, develop our character, and decide how we want to respond.
